# Modular Categories of Prime Power Dimension and Their Group-Theoretical Structure

The classification of modular categories according to their Frobenius–Perron dimension has emerged as a central problem in the theory of fusion categories, mirroring in many respects the classification problem for finite groups. In this context, a particularly tractable and illuminating class consists of modular categories whose Frobenius–Perron dimension is a prime power. We show that such categories admit a clean and complete characterization: every modular category of Frobenius–Perron dimension $p^n$ is equivalent, as a braided fusion category, to the representation category of a twisted double $D^\omega(G)$ of a finite $p$-group $G$, where $\omega$ is a 3-cocycle on $G$ encoding the associativity constraint. This result places such categories squarely within the framework of Drinfeld centers of pointed fusion categories, and it identifies the twisted quantum doubles of $p$-groups as the fundamental building blocks from which all prime-power-dimensional modular categories are constructed.

This classification is best understood within a broader structural theory of nilpotent braided fusion categories, which generalizes the notion of nilpotency from finite group theory to the categorical setting. Just as every finite nilpotent group decomposes canonically as a direct product of its Sylow $p$-subgroups, we establish that every nilpotent braided fusion category admits an analogous decomposition into "Sylow" braided fusion subcategories, each supported on objects whose dimensions are powers of a fixed prime. This categorical Sylow decomposition is compatible with the braiding and allows one to reduce many structural questions about nilpotent braided fusion categories to the prime-power case, in direct analogy with the reduction techniques used throughout finite group theory.

Within this framework, the interaction between nilpotency and integrality of dimensions plays a decisive role. Specifically, we prove that if $\mathcal{C}$ is a nilpotent braided fusion category all of whose simple objects have integer Frobenius–Perron dimension, then $\mathcal{C}$ is necessarily group-theoretical, meaning that it is categorically Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category, or equivalently, that it can be realized as a category of bimodules over a group algebra twisted by a cohomological class. This result significantly extends earlier partial results on the group-theoretical property of braided fusion categories and shows that, under the hypotheses of nilpotency and integrality, no genuinely new "exotic" braided structures can arise: the categorical data is entirely governed by finite group cohomology.

A notable consequence of this theorem concerns the theory of semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras. Since the representation category of any semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of prime power dimension is a fusion category that is automatically nilpotent (by a categorical analogue of the fact that groups of prime power order are nilpotent) and has integral dimensions for its simple objects, our integrality result applies directly. We conclude that every semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of dimension $p^n$ is group-theoretical, thereby extending the celebrated theorem of Etingof and Gelaki on semisimple Hopf algebras of prime power dimension to the more general quasi-Hopf setting, where associativity may be twisted by a nontrivial 3-cocycle.

The proofs of these results are unified by a common technical strategy: the reconstruction of twisted quantum doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories. Recall that a modular category $\mathcal{C}$ contains a Lagrangian subcategory $\mathcal{L}$ (a maximal isotropic subcategory with respect to the categorical braiding form) precisely when $\mathcal{C}$ arises as the Drinfeld center of a fusion category built from $\mathcal{L}$; in the prime power case, this fusion category can be shown to be pointed, and the corresponding modular category is thus identified with a twisted double $D^\omega(G)$. This reconstruction procedure is conceptually parallel to the classical correspondence between Manin triples (or, more generally, Manin pairs) and quasi-Lie bialgebras: just as a Lagrangian subalgebra of a Manin pair determines a Lie bialgebra structure via a Drinfeld double construction, a Lagrangian subcategory of a modular category determines the pointed fusion category whose center recovers the original modular category. This analogy provides not only a powerful heuristic guiding the categorical arguments but also the technical backbone for translating cohomological and group-theoretic information between the classical and categorical settings.

# Modular Categories of Prime Power Dimension and Group-Theoretical Structure

## Introduction

The classification of fusion categories according to their Frobenius-Perron dimension has been a central theme in the structure theory of tensor categories, paralleling analogous developments in finite group theory. Just as groups of prime power order enjoy remarkably rich structural properties—nilpotency, the existence of nontrivial centers, and various decomposition theorems—one expects fusion categories whose Frobenius-Perron dimension is a prime power to exhibit correspondingly strong structural constraints. This paper addresses this expectation directly in the setting of modular categories, establishing that modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension are completely classified as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite p-groups.

## Background and Motivation

Modular categories arise naturally in the study of topological quantum field theories, conformal field theory, and the representation theory of quantum groups at roots of unity. A fundamental class of examples is provided by the representation categories of twisted doubles $D^\omega(G)$ of finite groups $G$, where $\omega$ is a 3-cocycle on $G$ controlling the associativity constraints. When $G$ is a p-group, these categories have Frobenius-Perron dimension $|G|^2$, a power of $p$, making them natural candidates for a complete classification in the prime power setting.

A parallel and equally important line of investigation concerns semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras, whose representation categories are fusion categories. A quasi-Hopf algebra is called group-theoretical if its representation category is equivalent, as a fusion category, to a category constructed from a finite group and cohomological data—specifically, if it can be realized via the double coset construction from a finite group with a 3-cocycle and a subgroup with a compatible 2-cochain. Determining when semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras are group-theoretical has significant implications for their structure theory, including questions about their representation rings, module categories, and associated invariants.

## Methodology

The approach taken in this paper proceeds through several interconnected steps, each building toward the main classification result.

### Reconstruction from Lagrangian Subcategories

A key technical tool is the reconstruction of twisted doubles $D^\omega(G)$ from Lagrangian subcategories of the associated modular category. Given a modular category $\mathcal{C}$ that arises as the Drinfeld center of a fusion category, a Lagrangian subcategory provides a maximal isotropic subspace with respect to the natural symmetric form induced by the double braiding. The existence of such a subcategory, together with its structural properties, allows one to reconstruct the underlying group $G$ and cocycle $\omega$ explicitly from categorical data internal to $\mathcal{C}$. This reconstruction theorem serves as the technical backbone connecting abstract modular categories of the appropriate dimension to concrete twisted double constructions.

### Nilpotency and Sylow Decomposition

The second major component of the methodology involves establishing a Sylow-type decomposition theorem for nilpotent braided fusion categories. Building on the notion of nilpotency for fusion categories—defined via the existence of a tower of faithful gradings by cyclic groups of prime order terminating in the trivial category—the paper demonstrates that a nilpotent braided fusion category $\mathcal{B}$ decomposes as a Deligne tensor product of its Sylow subcategories:
$$\mathcal{B} \cong \boxtimes_p \mathcal{B}_p$$
where each $\mathcal{B}_p$ is a braided fusion category of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension. This decomposition mirrors the classical Sylow decomposition of nilpotent finite groups and reduces the study of general nilpotent braided fusion categories to the prime power case, which is precisely where the reconstruction theorem for twisted doubles becomes applicable.

## Main Results

Combining these two strands of investigation yields the paper's central classification theorem: every modular category of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension $p^n$ is equivalent, as a modular tensor category, to the representation category of a twisted double $D^\omega(G)$ for some finite p-group $G$ and 3-cocycle $\omega \in H^3(G, \mathbb{C}^\times)$.

This classification has an immediate and significant consequence for the group-theoretical property. The paper establishes that any such modular category with *integral* Frobenius-Perron dimensions—meaning the dimension of every simple object is an integer rather than merely an algebraic number—is necessarily group-theoretical in the sense of Ostrik and collaborators. This integrality condition, combined with the prime power constraint, forces sufficient rigidity that the category admits the group-theoretical realization via a canonical construction from finite group data.

## Consequences for Quasi-Hopf Algebras

The categorical classification translates directly into an algebraic statement about semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras. Since the representation category of a semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of dimension $p^n$ is a fusion category with integral Frobenius-Perron dimensions equal to $p^n$, and since the Drinfeld center of any fusion category is modular, the results above apply to the center of the representation category. The paper demonstrates that this categorical information can be leveraged to establish that the original quasi-Hopf algebra itself must be group-theoretical.

This resolves, in the prime power case, a natural analogue of results previously known for ordinary semisimple Hopf algebras. The result places semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension firmly within the group-theoretical framework, meaning their representation theory can be completely described in terms of finite group cohomology and subgroup data, without recourse to more exotic quasi-Hopf algebra constructions.

## Conclusion

By combining a reconstruction theorem for twisted doubles from Lagrangian subcategories with a Sylow decomposition theorem for nilpotent braided fusion categories, this paper achieves a complete structural classification of modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension. The consequence that such categories with integral dimensions are group-theoretical extends naturally to establish the group-theoretical property for semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension, providing a significant structural result that parallels and extends known theorems in the ordinary Hopf algebra setting. These results contribute to the broader program of understanding fusion and modular categories through group-theoretical and cohomological invariants, and open avenues for further investigation into the non-integral case and into nilpotent fusion categories of more general dimension.

# On the Interplay of Frobenius, Perron, and Sylow in Group Theory and Linear Algebra

Mathematics is rich with named theorems and structures that bear the imprint of their discoverers, and three such figures—Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, Oskar Perron, and Ludwig Sylow—have left legacies that intersect in surprising ways across algebra and analysis.

## Sylow's Theorems: The Architecture of Finite Groups

Ludwig Sylow, a Norwegian mathematician, revolutionized the study of finite groups in 1872 with his celebrated theorems concerning **Sylow subgroups**. These theorems guarantee the existence of subgroups whose order is the highest power of a prime dividing the order of a finite group, and they describe precisely how these subgroups relate to one another—all being conjugate, and their number satisfying specific congruence conditions modulo the prime in question. Sylow's work provides an essential toolkit for classifying finite groups, forming a cornerstone of group theory that remains central to modern algebra courses.

## Frobenius: A Bridge Between Algebra and Representation Theory

Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, a towering figure in 19th-century German mathematics, made profound contributions across multiple domains. In group theory, the **Frobenius theorem** on group extensions and **Frobenius groups** (transitive permutation groups with specific fixed-point properties) extended the structural insights that Sylow's theorems initiated. Frobenius also pioneered representation theory, connecting abstract group structures to matrices and linear transformations.

Notably, Frobenius's work often built directly upon Sylow-type reasoning—for instance, in proving results about the existence of subgroups of specific orders (the **Frobenius theorem on subgroup counting**), which generalizes ideas embedded in Sylow's original framework.

## Perron and the Theory of Positive Matrices

Oskar Perron, working independently in a different branch of mathematics, developed the **Perron-Frobenius theorem** together with Frobenius himself. This landmark result in linear algebra concerns the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of positive (or non-negative) matrices, showing that such matrices possess a unique largest eigenvalue with an associated eigenvector of positive entries. This theorem has become indispensable in:

- **Economics** (input-output models, Markov chains)
- **Google's PageRank algorithm**
- **Population dynamics**
- **Network theory**

## The Convergence of Ideas

Though Sylow's theorems belong to pure group theory and the Perron-Frobenius theorem to matrix analysis, both traditions converge in the broader Frobenius legacy. Frobenius's mathematical versatility—spanning finite group theory, representation theory, and matrix analysis—demonstrates how seemingly disparate areas of mathematics can be unified through a single mathematician's insight. The name Frobenius thus serves as a conceptual bridge between the **discrete world of Sylow's group-theoretic structures** and the **continuous world of Perron's spectral theory**, illustrating the deep interconnectedness of algebraic and analytic mathematics.

This trio of names continues to resonate in contemporary research, from computational group theory to network science, testament to the enduring power of 19th-century mathematical insight.

# On Nilpotent Braided Fusion Categories: Sylow Decomposition and Group-Theoretical Structure

## Abstract

We study the structure theory of nilpotent braided fusion categories, extending the classical theory of nilpotent groups and the Drinfeld center perspective on fusion categories to the braided setting. A fusion category $\mathcal{C}$ is called *nilpotent* if its universal grading group sequence terminates in the trivial category after finitely many steps of taking adjoint subcategories, and we consider this notion in the presence of a braiding, which imposes strong compatibility constraints between the grading and the ribbon/twist structure.

Our main results are twofold. First, we establish a **Sylow-type decomposition theorem**: every nilpotent braided fusion category $\mathcal{C}$ of Frobenius–Perron dimension $\mathrm{FPdim}(\mathcal{C}) = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$ factors as a Deligne tensor product
$$
\mathcal{C} \;\cong\; \mathcal{C}_{p_1} \boxtimes \mathcal{C}_{p_2} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \mathcal{C}_{p_k},
$$
where each $\mathcal{C}_{p_i}$ is a braided fusion category of dimension $p_i^{a_i}$, unique up to braided equivalence, and this decomposition is compatible with the ribbon structure when $\mathcal{C}$ is premodular. The proof proceeds by showing that the components of the universal grading corresponding to distinct primes centralize one another in the Müger sense, using the interplay between the nilpotency filtration and the nondegeneracy of the braiding on graded pieces, together with an inductive analysis of the core (the trivial component of the grading).

Second, building on this decomposition, we prove that **every integral nilpotent braided fusion category is group-theoretical**: it is obtained as a de-equivariantization/equivariantization or, equivalently, is categorically Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category, hence lies in the image of the Tambara–Yamagami-free construction from finite groups and 2-cocycles. The key step shows that each Sylow-type piece $\mathcal{C}_{p_i}$, being a nilpotent braided category of prime-power dimension, embeds into its own Drinfeld center as a Lagrangian-adjacent subcategory arising from a nilpotent group $p_i$-group action, allowing an inductive reduction (via de-equivariantization along central subgroups of the grading group) to categories of strictly smaller dimension. Combined with the multiplicativity of the group-theoretical property under Deligne products, this yields group-theoreticity of $\mathcal{C}$ in full.

As applications, we classify integral nilpotent modular categories of dimension $p^a q^b$ ($p,q$ prime) up to Witt equivalence, recovering and extending results on metaplectic and Ising-type categories, and we describe the associated Lagrangian subgroups explicitly in terms of the underlying nilpotent group data. We also discuss obstructions to the non-integral case, where quantum-dimension considerations prevent a direct analogue of group-theoreticity, and indicate connections to the classification of low-rank premodular categories.

**Keywords:** braided fusion category, nilpotent category, Sylow decomposition, group-theoretical category, modular tensor category, Müger centralizer, de-equivariantization

We investigate the structure of semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension, establishing that any such algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero is group-theoretical. Our approach exploits the correspondence between semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras and their representation categories, which are fusion categories, together with the reconstruction technique linking these categories to Lagrangian subcategories of modular tensor categories.

By the Drinfeld center construction, $Z(\mathrm{Rep}(H))$ yields a modular tensor category of dimension $p^{2n}$, within which $\mathrm{Rep}(H)$ embeds as a Lagrangian subcategory—that is, a subcategory whose objects have dimensions squaring to the total dimension and which is closed under the appropriate duality structure. This nilpotency, combined with results on the structure of solvable fusion categories, allows us to reconstruct $\mathrm{Rep}(H)$ as arising from a group-theoretical datum: a finite $p$-group $G$, a subgroup $K \leq G$, a $3$-cocycle $\omega \in H^3(G, \mathbb{C}^\times)$, and a $2$-cochain on $K$ trivializing the restriction of $\omega$.

# Abstract

We study the structure of modular tensor categories whose global (Frobenius-Perron) dimension is a prime power $p^n$. Building on the theory of nilpotent fusion categories and the Sylow decomposition of braided fusion categories established in earlier work, we show that every modular category $\mathcal{C}$ of dimension $p^n$ is nilpotent, and more precisely that $\mathcal{C}$ is group-theoretical: it is Morita equivalent (as a fusion category) to a pointed category, and hence to a category of representations of a twisted group algebra of a $p$-group. We prove that the Müger center of any fusion subcategory of $\mathcal{C}$ closed under the modular structure is again modular, and we use the Sylow theory for braided fusion categories to reduce the classification to the case of a single prime, showing that $\mathcal{C}$ decomposes as a Deligne product of modular categories of prime power dimension $p^{n_i}$ associated to the primes dividing its dimension. Central to our approach is the reconstruction and analysis of Lagrangian subcategories: we show that every modular category of dimension $p^{2n}$ that is not simple as a braided category contains a Lagrangian subcategory, and this containment governs the categorical Witt class and de-equivariantization of $\mathcal{C}$. Using this, we classify modular categories of dimension $p^2$ and $p^3$ completely, describe their fusion rules and $S$- and $T$-matrices, and show they arise from metric groups or their $\mathbb{Z}/2$-extensions. As an application, we establish that the Witt group of nondegenerate braided fusion categories of prime power dimension is generated by pointed categories, and we discuss consequences for the classification of low-rank modular categories and for the property of "weak integrality" in modular tensor categories arising in topological quantum field theory and anyon models.
